items.title: Michael Caine licenses voice to narrate AI adaptation Odyssey audiobook
items.summary: Michael Caine has licensed an AI-generated version of his voice to narrate an audiobook adaptation of Homer's Odyssey, produced with voice-AI company ElevenLabs. A marquee example of a major actor formally licensing (rather than fighting) an AI voice clone for a literary work, and a signal of where celebrity AI narration deals are heading. By Lisa Maru.
items.notes: Single-story product/deal news; verified on-page date June 24, 2026. Bookseller item 1 of 2.

items.title: Over 250 UK publishers opt in to collective AI licensing scheme
items.summary: Publishers' Licensing Services announced that more than 250 UK publishers have opted in to its collective AI licensing scheme, launched earlier in 2026 at London Book Fair. The scheme lets publishers collectively manage and monetize licensing of their content to AI companies — a concrete counter-model to unlicensed scraping. By Melina Spanoudi.
items.notes: Single-story industry news; verified on-page date June 24, 2026. Bookseller item 2 of 2.

items.title: Amazon Kindle and Kindle Scribe 5.19.5 Update Released
items.summary: Amazon's firmware 5.19.5 for Kindle and Kindle Scribe rolls out 'Story So Far' — spoiler-free recaps up to your current reading position for thousands of English-language books — plus improved Scribe annotation tools and cross-device bookmarking. Story So Far extends Amazon's AI-generated Recaps feature (introduced 2025) from series level to in-book progress. By Michael Kozlowski.
items.notes: Verified on-page date June 30, 2026. Article does not label the feature 'AI' explicitly, but Story So Far/Recaps is Amazon's AI-generated recap line; writer should frame carefully. Distinct from the already-published Kindle Translate card.

items.title: BISG, BookNet Canada Launch 2026 'AI in the Book Industry' Survey
items.summary: The Book Industry Study Group and BookNet Canada opened their second annual 'AI in the Book Industry' survey (open through July 17) for publishing professionals across North America. The 2025 edition found AI use 'uneven and often exploratory' and sentiment 'overwhelmingly negative' — the industry adopting AI faster than it gets comfortable with it. By Andrew Albanese.
items.notes: Verified on-page date June 22, 2026 — at the edge of the 336h window (cutoff 2026-06-22T00:15Z). Single-story, actionable (survey open to July 17).

items.title: A Platform Comes Apart: Part 1
items.summary: Hong Zhou and Adam Hyde argue that autonomous AI agents are splitting scholarly publishing platforms into a 'trusted core' database layer and a separate 'agentic layer' where agents — not humans staring at yesterday's interface — do the interacting. The shift undermines per-seat SaaS pricing and forces vendors to rethink where platform value accumulates.
